Give every clause its own verb.
Do not leave a verb out of a clause and let the reader copy it from the clause before.
Linguists call this omission *gapping*, a kind of *ellipsis*: <!-- no-figure: grammatical ellipsis, not the conic -->
in "statistics calls it the intercept, and machine learning the bias", <!-- check-term-links: allow: a quoted example; "bias" here names an intercept, not the estimator bias that def-bias defines -->
the second clause has lost "calls it".
A clause that has lost its verb and everything after it,
as in "statistics calls it the intercept, and machine learning too",
has the same problem.

A reader has to notice the gap, find the verb it stands for, and carry it over.
A reader who is learning English may not see the gap at all,
and may read "machine learning the bias" as a phrase about learning. <!-- check-term-links: allow: quotes the example above; "bias" here names an intercept, not the estimator bias -->
Writing the verb out costs a word or two.

::: {#exm-dropped-verb}

## Restoring a dropped verb

From a definition of the offset of an [affine map](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/linear-algebra-linear-maps.html#def-affine-map), in the mds notes:

> ❌ In the definition of an affine map, the vector $\vec{b}$ is called the offset of $f$
> (statistics also calls it the intercept, and machine learning the bias). <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted ❌ example; "bias" here names an intercept, not the estimator bias -->

>
> ✅ In the definition of an affine map, the vector $\vb$ is called the offset of $f$.
> Statistics also calls it the intercept, and machine learning calls it the bias. <!-- check-term-links: allow: quoted ✅ example; "bias" here names an intercept, not the estimator bias -->

From a proof about chains of inequalities, in the mcs notes:

> ❌ So two steps that are each $\le$ or $<$ give $<$ if either is $<$, and otherwise $\le$.
>
> ✅ So two steps that are each $\le$ or $<$ give $<$ if either is $<$, and they give $\le$ otherwise.

In each ✅ version, every clause has its own verb,
so the reader does not have to copy one across.

:::

The rule is about clauses, not about lists.
One verb can take several subjects or several objects in a single clause:
"Statistics and machine learning both use the [term](defining-terms.qmd#def-term)" has one clause and one verb.
One subject can also take several verbs, each written out:
"The lasso shrinks the coefficients and sets some of them to zero."
A short verb such as "does" can stand in for a verb phrase in the same sentence,
as in "Ridge regression shrinks the coefficients, and the lasso does too",
because the reader still sees a verb in each clause.

This rule covers words left out of a sentence.
The ellipsis mark for the omitted terms of a sequence belongs in math, as in $x_1, \ldots, x_n$. <!-- no-figure: the punctuation mark, not the conic -->
The section [Do not clip a term](inclusive-writing.qmd#do-not-clip-a-term) in the inclusive-writing chapter covers words left out of a technical term.
